newsitem.title: CANADA: DiamondWorks starts mining diamonds in Angola.
newsitem.headline: DiamondWorks starts mining diamonds in Angola.

text.p: Canada's DiamondWorks Ltd said Tuesday it started mining diamonds in war-torn Angola, a landmark in the sometimes controversial company's effort to transform itself into a major gem producer.
DiamondWorks said it has begun dredging alluvial deposits at its 48 percent-held Luo property in Angola's diamond-rich province of Lunda Norte.

"The start of production at Luo marks an important milestone for DiamondWorks. At this time, we remain on schedule to begin full-scale commercial production in Angola in May," Chief Executive Officer Eric Friedland said.

Working under an accord with the Angolan state diamond company Endiama, the firm claims to be among the first foreign mining companies to exploit Angola's vast high-quality diamond resources since a 1994 peace agreement.

During Angola's 20-year civil war, UNITA rebels and others actively mined diamonds. Now as the country seeks to rebuild, foreign companies are scrambling for prospective ground, drawn by Angola's rank as one of the world's top diamond producers.

DiamondWorks views the start of commercial production as a key step and said revenues will help advance exploration. It aims to generate cash flow of more than US$400,000 a day from production of up to 1,500 carats daily by year end.
"The reality of alluvial production is we can do it right now and establish a very strong and quick cash flow," Friedland said in a recent interview.

The company was born last year when Friedland, brother of successful mining financier Robert Friedland, reshaped Vancouver-listed Carson Gold Corp. Carson, which had focused on Venezuelan gold exploration, bought the diamond assets of Branch Energy Ltd in Africa and renamed itself DiamondWorks.
Branch Energy's chairman Tony Buckingham became the company's controlling shareholder through the deal, receiving about a 50 percent stake in DiamondWorks for the properties.

The company has projects in Sierra Leone, Canada and China but its three Angolan concessions are its chief attraction. As for Luo, "the concession is vast and the potential is vast," said DiamondWorks Director Michael Grunberg.
"Luo is regarded as arguably the key alluvial concession with two of the top 10 (kimberlite) pipes (in Angola)...These stones are spectacular," he said.
DiamondWorks, which has proven, probable and inferred reserves of about 22 million carats on all its properties, is focusing on the most lucrative gem sector.

Some investors have been leery of DiamondWorks' forays into countries like Angola and Sierra Leone which have been riven by conflict. But DiamondWorks insists the risks are not as high as many outsiders believe and said the discount factor applied by analysts who value its properties is too great.
"On the ground, your confidence grows," Friedland said. "We're trendsetters....Others will follow suit."

Antwerp diamond consultant Luc Rombouts agreed that Angola's potential is enormous but said the drawbacks, including tough operating conditions, insecurity, corruption and potential threats to title should not be underestimated.
"It's very hard working there -- so corrupt and you spend so much," he said. "There are very rich deposits but...you never know what is going to happen next.

DiamondWorks has also been dogged by controversy because of Buckingham's friendships with principals of Executive Outcomes, a South African firm staffed by many former soldiers from the apartheid era that sells military services to governments.

According to a DiamondWorks prospectus, Buckingham provides introductions for the Executive Outcomes and an Executives Outcomes' affiliate handles security for DiamondWorks in Sierra Leone. The connection has prompted extensive media coverage questioning the ethics of the arrangement.

But DiamondWorks insists that it and Branch Energy have no corporate links with Executive Outcomes. Moreover, it said investors welcome the company's use of private security forces at operations in Africa, where such measures are considered necessary.
((-- Reuters Vancouver Bureau (604) 664-7314))
